catalog_quote: 3.6.6. Developments of vowels due to stress. The change from the PIE tonal accent to a (heavy) initial stress in all likelihood occurred during the Proto-Italic period (cf. Meiser 1998:66). The developments of the vowels due to this initial stress are of later date, however: both the weakening of vowels and the syncopation in medial and final syllables do not seem to have taken place before the sixth century and to have been completed by the fifth (Rix 1966, Meiser 1998:66-7). There are hardly any indications of vowel-weakening or syncopation in Faliscan, and Faliscan is indeed notorious for not having vowel-weakening (a point that is repeated from author to author). ... All in all, the instances of syncopation in internal syllables appear to show that the phenomenon did occur in Middle and Late Faliscan, but irregularly. ... Resuming the point that was made at the beginning of this sec…

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the scanned file we hold at the stated lines/pages, and is now also verified in the author's text-layer PDF of Bakkum 2009 ch.3 (pp.100, 103), downloaded today from UvA-DARE together with every other chapter. (2) Deciding source: Bakkum 2009 is the definitive modern grammar-cum-corpus of Faliscan (678 pp., 65-pp. phonology chapter); nothing better exists, and the Glottolog list offers no Faliscan-specific phonology beyond it. Its sec. 3.6.6 gives only a hedged Proto-Italic initial-stress inheritance plus irregular Middle/Late Faliscan medial syncope as evidence that 'stress did affect the vowels'; no accent position is stated for attested Faliscan, and a full-text search for stress/accent all other chapters finds none. Rigobianco 2020 (held) and Nishimura 2014 (held under osca1245) are silent. For an epigraphic corpus language whose script does not mark accent, UNDETERM

sources.quote: Reports that Mercado 'assumes the Plautine accent rules' for his stress-based Saturnian schema, that Parsons' model has the Saturnian develop 'while Latin had word-initial stress', and that Mercado 'determines that the Faliscan Cooks' Dedication (CIL I2 364) is in fact in Saturnians (196-199)'. Second-hand; an analytic assumption for verse, not a description of Faliscan stress.

sources.note: Only monograph that scans the Faliscan (and Faliscan-Latin) verse inscriptions with a stress-based metre, so it must commit to an accent placement for 3rd-2nd c. Faliscan (BMCR: Plautine accent rules assumed; Cooks' Dedication CIL I2 364 pp.196-199); would let the 'undetermined' note say whether any metrical evidence for initial vs Latin-type accent in attested Faliscan has been claimed. Would not by itself license a positional code (assumption, not description).
